631.title: Come, Lord Jesus (Apocalypse 22:17–21)
631.carry: take the water of life, freely
631.howItsDone: Catholics voice this longing at every Mass, in the prayer after the Lord's Prayer that speaks of waiting for the coming of the Savior, and especially in Advent, the season of preparing for Christ's coming; some pray maranatha as a short, repeated prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tabernacle: the city coming down, and every tear wiped away. Your line was behold, I make all things new. Who did you comfort? Day six hundred thirty-one.

Back on day three hundred thirty-two, we opened a library, not a book, and started at the first page: in the beginning. Since then, Genesis, the kings, the prophets, the psalms, the Gospels, the letters, the visions. Today we turn the last page. And the Bible doesn't end with a summary, or a moral, or a final warning. It ends with a conversation. Someone says come. Someone answers I'm coming. And then the last prayer in the whole book, three words long. An older form of it turns up in one of Paul's letters, in another language.
screen: `THE LAST PAGE OF THE LIBRARY.` → `NOT A SUMMARY: A CONVERSATION.` → `THE BIBLE'S LAST PRAYER.`

segments.voice: First, in the Douay-Rheims: "And the spirit and the bride say: Come. And he that heareth, let him say: Come." The Spirit and the bride, the Church, call out to Christ. Then the invitation turns around, toward anyone listening: let him that thirsts come, and take the water of life, freely. Come goes both ways. Then Christ answers: "Surely I come quickly: Amen. Come, Lord Jesus." That's the Bible's last prayer. Come, Lord Jesus. Now go back to Paul. Writing in Greek to the Corinthians, he leaves one Aramaic word untranslated: maranatha. Aramaic was the language of Jesus and his first followers in Galilee. Paul keeps the word the way you'd keep a word from a grandmother's language, because no other word feels right. It can be read two ways, and scholars discuss which: maran atha, our Lord has come; or marana tha, our Lord, come! Christians can pray both. He has come; come again. An early Christian handbook called the Didache puts maranatha in its prayers after the Eucharist. And come, Lord Jesus, in the Apocalypse, sounds, to some scholars, like that same old prayer, put into Greek. The Bible ends, finally, with a blessing: "The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen." Catholics pray this longing at every Mass. After the Lord's Prayer, the priest prays for the people as they wait in hope for the coming of our Savior. And all through Advent, the Church sings come. The book whose first page has God saying let there be light ends with his people saying come.
screen: `THE SPIRIT AND THE BRIDE SAY: COME.` · `SURELY I COME QUICKLY.` · `MARANATHA: OUR LORD, COME.` · `PRAYED AT EVERY MASS AND IN ADVENT.` · then, large: `AMEN. COME, LORD JESUS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray come, Lord Jesus, or sit with the longing. Sit comfortably and breathe slowly. Think of what in your life, or in the world, most needs to be made new: a sorrow, a war, an illness, a relationship. Hold it gently. If you pray, you can say the Bible's last prayer on each out-breath: come, Lord Jesus. Or the old Aramaic word: maranatha, four soft syllables, ma-ra-na-tha. Let it slow down until it's almost a whisper. If you don't pray, just let yourself feel what it's like to long for something to come. The bell holds the time.
Maranatha. Aramaic, from the first Christians: our Lord, come, or our Lord has come. The Bible's last prayer. Today's word.

Your line: take the water of life, freely. Today, pause once and drink something slowly, water if you can, and let it remind you of the invitation. And that's the Apocalypse: an unveiling, the first and the last, first charity, not lukewarm, the knock, holy, the Lamb, every tongue, the woman, Babylon, the supper, tabernacle, and maranatha. The last page. Day six hundred thirty-one.

632.title: How the calendar works
632.hook: solemnities, feasts and memorials, with Sundays at the center
632.howItsDone: Catholics follow the General Roman Calendar, which ranks each day as a solemnity, feast, memorial or weekday; parish calendars, missals and liturgy apps show each day's rank and color.

segments.voice: Yesterday we reached the last page of the Bible: Maranatha, take the water of life, freely. The book, read in order, is done. Where did that old prayer find you? Day six hundred thirty-two.

Open a Catholic wall calendar, the free kind a parish hands out in December, and the squares are not all equal. Some days are printed in red. Some have a saint's name in small type. Some just say Tuesday of the twenty-third week. A few say something stronger, and the whole parish knows it: Christmas, Easter, the Assumption. We just finished reading the Bible in order, cover to cover. Now we read it the way the Church actually hears it, one feast at a time, around a year that has its own shape. Before we start, a key to the map. Today's word is the top rank.
screen: `NOT EVERY SQUARE IS EQUAL.` → `FROM THE BOOK TO THE YEAR.` → `A KEY TO THE MAP.`

segments.voice: The Church's calendar sorts its days into ranks. At the top is a solemnity, from the Latin sollemnitas, a yearly, festive observance. Christmas, Easter, Pentecost, the Immaculate Conception, Saints Peter and Paul. A solemnity begins the evening before, the way a Jewish sabbath begins at sunset, and at Mass the Gloria is sung and the Creed is said. One step down is a feast: an apostle, the Holy Family, the Conversion of Saint Paul. A feast keeps to its own day, with the Gloria and usually without the Creed. Below that comes a memorial, a saint remembered, some obligatory, some optional. And under them all, the plain weekday, which the books call a feria. Here's the surprise. Sunday sits at the center of the whole system. The Second Vatican Council called the Lord's Day the original feast day, kept every week in memory of the resurrection. An ordinary Sunday outranks almost every saint. The Sundays of Advent, Lent and Easter outrank even most solemnities: when one collides with them, the solemnity moves to another day. There's an official table, a ladder of thirteen steps, that settles every collision. It sounds like bookkeeping, and partly it is. But the effect is that the year breathes: long green stretches of ordinary weeks, then the purple seasons of waiting, then white and gold for the great days. A psalm the Church sings at Easter says it plainly: "This is the day which the Lord hath made: let us be glad and rejoice therein." The calendar is a way of saying which joy today is. And the year doesn't start in January. It starts tomorrow, with Advent.
screen: `SOLEMNITY: THE TOP RANK.` · `FEAST, MEMORIAL, WEEKDAY.` · `SUNDAY AT THE CENTER.` · `A YEAR THAT BREATHES.` · then, large: `THIS IS THE DAY WHICH THE LORD HATH MADE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find today's rank. If you have a missal, a parish calendar or a liturgy app, look up today. Is it a solemnity, a feast, a memorial, or a plain weekday? Is a saint named? What color is the priest wearing? If you can't look it up, simply guess, and check later. Then sit with whatever you found. A plain weekday is not a lesser day; most of life is lived on them. If you pray, you can greet today by its name. If you don't, just notice that it has one. The bell holds the time.
Solemnity. The highest rank of day in the Catholic calendar, from the Latin sollemnitas, a festive yearly observance. It begins the evening before. Today's word.
Your line: every day has a rank. Today, tell one person what kind of day it is in the Church's calendar, even if the answer is just Tuesday. Day six hundred thirty-two.

633.title: First Sunday of Advent (Mark 13:33–37)
633.hook: the new year starts with watch
633.howItsDone: On the First Sunday of Advent, Catholic churches begin the new liturgical year in violet vestments, and many parishes and families light the first candle of an Advent wreath.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the key to the calendar: solemnities, feasts, memorials, and Sunday at the center. Your line was every day has a rank. What rank did your day turn out to have? Day six hundred thirty-three.

New Year's Eve has a countdown and a party. The Church's new year begins on a Sunday in late November or early December, in purple, with a single candle and a warning. No fireworks. The first gospel of the year is not a birth story. It's about a house at night, a master who has gone away, and a doorkeeper told to stay awake. In the year when Mark's Gospel is read on Sundays, these five verses, Mark 13:33 to 37, open everything. Today the year turns over, and its first word is a command.
screen: `A NEW YEAR IN PURPLE.` → `A HOUSE AT NIGHT.` → `THE FIRST WORD IS A COMMAND.`

segments.voice: Advent comes from the Latin adventus, a coming or an arrival. Across the Sundays before Christmas, the Church looks two ways at once: back to the first coming, the birth in Bethlehem, and forward to the coming at the end of time. The first Sunday leans hard forward. In Mark, Jesus tells a small story. A man goes on a long journey. He leaves his house in his servants' hands, gives each one a job, and tells the porter at the door to keep watch. Nobody knows when he'll be back: in the evening, at midnight, at cockcrow, or in the morning. Four times, named one after another, so every hour of the dark is covered. Don't let him come suddenly and find you sleeping. Then the last line, which Mark aims past the disciples at every reader: "And what I say to you, I say to all: Watch." The Greek word is grēgoreite, stay awake, keep alert. It's a word for staying up when sleep would be easier. Notice what it doesn't say. It doesn't say panic, or calculate the date, or stare at the sky. Each servant has work. Watching, in this story, looks like doing your job well while staying awake to who might walk through the door. That's why the Church starts its year here. Before the manger, before the shepherds and the star, the first thing asked is attention. Then on this Sunday, in some homes, someone lights the first of four candles on a wreath, and the room has one small flame against the dark.
screen: `ADVENT: A COMING.` · `THE MASTER GOES AWAY.` · `FOUR WATCHES OF THE NIGHT.` · `WATCHING LOOKS LIKE WORK.` · then, large: `WHAT I SAY TO YOU, I SAY TO ALL: WATCH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: light one candle. If you have an Advent wreath, light the first candle. If not, any candle will do, or a single lamp in a dark room. Sit where you can see the flame. Watch it the way a doorkeeper watches a door: awake, unhurried, ready. When your mind wanders, come back to the light. If you pray, you can say the old word of Advent, take the water of life, freely. If you don't, just keep watch with the flame. The bell holds the time.
Gregoreite, stay awake. Mark thirteen: the Church's new year begins with a house at night and a porter told to keep watch. Today's word.
Your line: watch. Today, at one ordinary task, stay fully awake to it, and to whoever walks through your door. Day six hundred thirty-three.

634.title: Advent with Isaiah
634.hook: Advent's first readings come mostly from Isaiah: a people that walked in darkness
634.howItsDone: Through Advent, the first reading at Mass is very often from Isaiah, and Isaiah 9 is read at the Mass during the night of Christmas.

segments.voice: Yesterday, gregoreite: a house at night and a porter told to stay awake. Your line was one word, watch. What did you catch, being awake? Day six hundred thirty-four.

Sit in the pew on a weekday in early Advent and listen to the first reading. Day after day, the reader opens with the same words: a reading from the book of the prophet Isaiah. Swords beaten into plowshares. A wolf lying down with a lamb. A shoot from a stump. The desert blooming. Isaiah is the voice the Church hands Advent, so much that some people call him the Advent prophet. And the Isaiah line the Church saves for Christmas night is about people in the dark.
screen: `A READING FROM ISAIAH.` → `PLOWSHARES, WOLF, SHOOT.` → `PEOPLE IN THE DARK.`

segments.voice: Isaiah preached in Jerusalem in the days of King Ahaz and King Hezekiah. His world was frightening: Assyria, the great power of the day, was swallowing the small kingdoms around Judah, and Isaiah himself names the northern lands of Zebulun and Naphtali, up by the Sea of Galilee, as the ones brought low. Into that darkness Isaiah speaks a sentence in the past tense, as if the rescue had already happened. The Douay-Rheims reads: "The people that walked in darkness, have seen a great light." Light is risen, he says, on those in the region of the shadow of death. Then a child: a son is given, and the government will rest on his shoulder, and his names pile up, ending with Prince of Peace. Jewish readers place this in Isaiah's own time, and some Jewish commentators have understood the child as a king of Judah, Hezekiah. Christians read it as well as a promise fulfilled in Jesus, and Matthew's Gospel quotes the darkness-and-light line when Jesus begins preaching in Galilee, the very region Isaiah named. Both readings live with the same words. Why give Isaiah to Advent? Because Advent is about waiting in the dark without pretending it's already bright. Isaiah never says the darkness is small. He says a light shows up inside it. And Catholics hear this passage at the Mass during the night of Christmas, so Advent's prophet gets the first word of Christmas too. In early December the nights in the northern half of the world keep getting longer. The readings answer the calendar with one stubborn sentence.
screen: `ASSYRIA AND THE DARK NORTH.` · `A GREAT LIGHT, IN THE PAST TENSE.` · `A CHILD, A SON, A PRINCE OF PEACE.` · `SAVED FOR CHRISTMAS NIGHT.` · then, large: `THE PEOPLE THAT WALKED IN DARKNESS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read Isaiah 9:2, slowly, once. If you have a Bible nearby, find it. If not, hold the line you just heard: the people that walked in darkness have seen a great light. Then sit. Bring to mind one dark place you know, in your own life or in the news, without fixing it. Just let the sentence sit beside it. If you pray, you can hold that place up in the light. If you don't, simply keep both in view. The bell holds the time.
Hezekiah, a king of Judah. Isaiah's child oracle, read by Jewish tradition as this king, and by Christians as a promise fulfilled in Jesus. Today's word.
Your line: a great light. Today, notice the first light you switch on after dark, and let it remind you of Isaiah's sentence. Day six hundred thirty-four.

635.title: The Immaculate Conception (8 December)
635.hook: readings from Genesis 3 and the Annunciation
635.carry: full of grace from the start
635.howItsDone: Catholics keep December 8 as a solemnity, a holy day of obligation in many countries, with readings from Genesis 3 and Luke's account of the Annunciation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hezekiah, and a line for the long nights: a great light. Did you notice the first light you switched on after dark? Day six hundred thirty-five.

Ask a room of people what the Immaculate Conception is, and someone will probably say: it's when Jesus was conceived without a human father. It's an easy mix-up to make. But that's the virgin birth, a different teaching. December 8 is about Mary herself, and about the first moment of her own life. In the middle of Advent, nine months before her birthday on September 8, the Church stops for a solemnity. And the readings it chooses go all the way back to a garden.
screen: `NOT THE VIRGIN BIRTH.` → `MARY'S OWN BEGINNING.` → `BACK TO A GARDEN.`

segments.voice: The first reading is Genesis 3. Adam and Eve have eaten the fruit and hidden. God walks in the garden and calls, where art thou? Then God speaks to the serpent, in the Douay-Rheims: "I will put enmities between thee and the woman, and thy seed and her seed: she shall crush thy head." She, in that translation, because the Latin Vulgate says ipsa. The Hebrew points instead to the woman's offspring, he or it. Either way, Catholic tradition hears in this verse a first promise: a woman and her child, and a struggle with evil that ends in victory. Then the gospel jumps to Nazareth. The angel Gabriel greets a young woman: "Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee." Full of grace translates one Greek word, kecharitōmenē, a form that suggests favor already given and still lasting. In 1854, Pope Pius IX defined what Catholics had long celebrated: that Mary, from the first instant of her conception, was kept free of original sin, by a singular grace, in view of what her son would do. Not because she earned it, and not apart from Christ, but as the first fruit of his work. Put the two readings side by side and the shape appears: Eve, who reached for the fruit in the garden, and Mary, who would say be it done to me, in Nazareth. Christian traditions differ here. Orthodox Christians honor Mary as all-holy but generally don't accept the teaching in this defined form, and Protestant churches generally don't teach it. For Catholics it's a holy day, and in the United States, Mary under this title is the nation's patroness.
screen: `GENESIS 3: SHE SHALL CRUSH.` · `HAIL, FULL OF GRACE.` · `1854: FREE FROM THE FIRST INSTANT.` · `EVE IN THE GARDEN, MARY IN NAZARETH.` · then, large: `FULL OF GRACE FROM THE START.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one Hail Mary, slowly. If you pray, say it once, aloud or silently. It opens with the angel's own greeting, and then Elizabeth's, before it asks anything. Let each phrase land before the next. If you don't pray, sit with the angel's greeting itself, full of grace, and think of a beginning in your own life that was a gift, something you didn't earn. Then rest in the quiet. The bell holds the time.
Kecharitomene, full of grace. The angel's name for Mary in Luke one: favor already given, and still lasting, kept on December eighth. Today's word.
Your line: full of grace from the start. Today, if someone mixes up the Immaculate Conception and the virgin birth, you'll know the difference. Day six hundred thirty-five.

636.title: Our Lady of Guadalupe (12 December)
636.hook: the patroness of the Americas; roses in December
636.howItsDone: On December 12 many Catholics, especially Mexican and Mexican-American communities, gather before dawn to sing Las Mañanitas to Our Lady of Guadalupe and bring roses to her image.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kecharitomene: not the virgin birth, but Mary herself, full of grace from the start. Did anyone mix them up around you? Day six hundred thirty-six.

Before dawn on December 12, in Mexico City and in parishes from Los Angeles to Chicago, people gather outside churches to sing Las Mañanitas, the birthday song, to Mary. Mariachis in the dark. Roses everywhere, in buckets, in arms, in front of a framed image of a young woman with her head bowed, dressed in a starred mantle, standing on a crescent moon. Her basilica in Mexico City stands at the foot of a hill. The story behind all those roses begins with a poor man on that hill in winter.
screen: `SINGING IN THE DARK.` → `ROSES EVERYWHERE.` → `A MAN ON A HILL.`

segments.voice: December 1531, in the years just after the Spanish conquest of the Aztec capital. Juan Diego, an Indigenous man and a recent convert, is walking past the hill of Tepeyac. He hears birdsong, then a voice calling him by name. A young woman, speaking his own language, Nahuatl, tells him she is the Mother of the true God and asks for a church to be built there. He goes to the bishop, Juan de Zumárraga, who is unconvinced and asks for a sign. Then Juan Diego's uncle falls gravely ill, and Juan Diego, embarrassed, takes a different path around the hill to fetch a priest and avoid her. She meets him anyway. The best-known account gives her words, in paraphrase: do not be afraid; am I not here, I who am your mother? She tells him his uncle is already healed and sends him up the hill, where in the cold of December he finds roses blooming. He gathers them into his tilma, his rough cloak, and carries them to the bishop. When he opens it, the roses fall, and on the cloth is the image people still visit today. The fullest account, the Nican Mopohua, was published in Nahuatl in 1649, and historians debate how early the story was written down; the Church's devotion rests on long tradition and on the image itself. In 2002, Pope John Paul II canonized Juan Diego. Popes have named Mary under this title patroness of the Americas. In the story, notice who she chooses: not the bishop, but a conquered man, addressed in his own tongue, by name.
screen: `TEPEYAC, DECEMBER 1531.` · `THE BISHOP ASKS FOR A SIGN.` · `AM I NOT HERE?` · `ROSES IN THE TILMA.` · then, large: `I WHO AM YOUR MOTHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bring a flower to a church, or plan to. If there's a church near you, picture the walk, the door, the place by an image of Mary where people leave roses. If you can go today, take one flower. For now, sit and think of someone who has said to you, in their own way, I'm here. A parent, a friend, a stranger in a hard hour. If you pray, you can offer that person and that flower to Our Lady. If you don't, simply give thanks for them. The bell holds the time.
Nican Mopohua, 'here it is told.' The Nahuatl account of Mary's appearance to Juan Diego at Tepeyac in 1531, published in 1649. Today's word.
Your line: am I not here. Today, be the one who shows up for someone who's taking the long way around. Day six hundred thirty-six.

637.title: Gaudete Sunday (Philippians 4:4)
637.hook: the rose candle: rejoice, the Lord is near
637.howItsDone: On the third Sunday of Advent many Catholic parishes light the rose candle of the Advent wreath, and the priest may wear rose vestments instead of violet.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nican Mopohua: roses in December and a question that's also a promise, am I not here. Who showed up for you, or did you show up for? Day six hundred thirty-seven.

Look at an Advent wreath in its third week. Two purple candles have burned down a little. Then there's one that isn't purple at all. It's pink, or as the Church calls it, rose. On the third Sunday of Advent the priest may wear rose vestments too, a color that appears only twice a year. People who don't know the reason sometimes think the florist got the order wrong. The real reason is one Latin word, the first word sung at that Sunday's Mass for many centuries. Today's word.
screen: `TWO PURPLE, THEN ONE ROSE.` → `ONLY TWICE A YEAR.` → `ONE LATIN WORD.`

segments.voice: Gaudete means rejoice, said to more than one person. It opens the entrance chant of the third Sunday of Advent, taken from Paul's letter to the Philippians. In the Douay-Rheims: "Rejoice in the Lord always; again, I say, rejoice." And the reason follows a verse later: "The Lord is nigh." Here's what gives it weight. Paul wrote this letter in chains. He mentions his bonds again and again, and he isn't sure he'll leave prison alive. So this isn't a cheerful man telling everyone to smile. It's a prisoner insisting that joy has a source outside his circumstances. Advent is a season of waiting, and waiting can turn grim. So halfway through, the Church lightens the color. Purple softens to rose, as if the first light of dawn were showing at the edge of the sky. It isn't Christmas yet. The waiting isn't over. But the nearness has started to show. Gaudete Sunday ends a week that has walked a long way. It opened with the Bible's last prayer, Maranatha, take the water of life, freely. Then we learned that every day has a rank. The new year began with one word, watch. Isaiah gave us a great light. Kecharitomene gave us full of grace from the start. Guadalupe gave us am I not here. And now rose, and rejoice. Read them in a row and they form a small Advent all their own: a cry, a calendar, a lookout, a light, a girl, a mother, and joy on the way.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wear something bright. Before you sit, if you can, put on one bright thing: a scarf, a pair of socks, a ring, a pink shirt you never wear. Then sit with it on. Notice one honest reason for joy today, even small, even alongside something hard, the way Paul found his in chains. Don't force a feeling. Just name the reason. If you pray, you can say Paul's words, rejoice in the Lord always. If you don't, simply let the color remind you. The bell holds the time.
Gaudete. Latin for rejoice, said to many. It names the third Sunday of Advent, with its rose candle and rose vestments. Today's word.
Your line: rejoice. Today, wear your bright thing where someone can see it, and if they ask, tell them it's Gaudete. Day six hundred thirty-seven.
